title: The Courage of Bilal
subtitle: Unbending Faith, 'Ahad Ahad', and Emancipation by Abu Bakr
summary: The early acceptance of Islam by Bilal ibn Rabah, his brutal torment in the desert of al-Batha by Umayyah ibn Khalaf, his immortal cry of 'Ahad! Ahad!', his liberation by Abu Bakr al-Siddiq, and his enduring legacy as the first Mu'adhin of Islam.

sections.text: Bilal ibn Rabah: Dignity in Bondage

Among the most revered figures in Islamic history is Bilal ibn Rabah al-Habashi. Ibn Ishaq describes him as born into slavery among Banu Jumah; his mother was named Hamamah. He was owned by Umayyah ibn Khalaf, a wealthy chief of that clan.
Bilal accepted Islam early. In the report of 'Abdullah ibn Mas'ud in Sunan Ibn Majah, he is named among the first seven people to show their Islam openly in Makkah.
The Ordeal in the Sands of al-Batha
When Umayyah ibn Khalaf learned that his slave had accepted Islam, he set out to force him back to the religion of Quraysh.

Ibn Mas'ud's report relates that they handed Bilal over to the boys of Makkah, who led him around the mountain passes of the city while he kept saying, 'Ahad, Ahad.' Other sirah reports add that a rope was tied around his neck.

Ibn Ishaq relates that when the midday heat was at its most intense, Umayyah would take Bilal out, throw him on his back on the open ground of Makkah, and then order a large rock to be placed on his chest.
The harsh, sun-baked desert expanses around Makkah where Bilal endured torture.
The Immortal Proclamation: 'Ahad! Ahad!'
Then, Ibn Ishaq continues, Umayyah would say to him: 'You will stay like this until you die, or until you disbelieve in Muhammad and worship al-Lat and al-'Uzza.'

Bilal's answer, as Ibn Ishaq and Ibn Mas'ud both relate, was a single repeated word affirming the oneness of God: 'Ahad! Ahad!' (One! One!). Ibn Mas'ud's report notes that he alone among those tortured did not give his tormentors what they demanded.
"Ahad! Ahad!" (One! One!) — Bilal ibn Rabah, as related by Ibn Ishaq (Sirah of Ibn Hisham) and in Sunan Ibn Majah, Hadith 150

Ibn Ishaq relates, from Hisham ibn 'Urwah from his father without a connected chain, that Waraqah ibn Nawfal passed by while Bilal was being tortured and said, 'One, One, by God, O Bilal,' and then swore to Umayyah and his people that if they killed him for this, he would take his grave as a place of mercy. This report is difficult to reconcile with Sahih al-Bukhari, which states that Waraqah died soon after the first revelation, before the open call to Islam and the persecution of Bilal. It should therefore be treated with caution.
Emancipation by Abu Bakr al-Siddiq

Ibn Ishaq relates that Abu Bakr al-Siddiq passed by while Bilal was being tortured and said to Umayyah: 'Do you not fear God concerning this poor man? How long will you go on?' Umayyah replied: 'You are the one who corrupted him, so save him from what you see.'

In Ibn Ishaq's account, Abu Bakr answered that he would: he had a black slave who was stronger and sturdier than Bilal and who followed Umayyah's religion, and he offered him in exchange. Umayyah accepted, and Abu Bakr took Bilal and freed him. Other reports describe the purchase as made with money, and the amounts given in them differ.
Ibn Ishaq names Bilal as one of seven believers persecuted in Makkah whom Abu Bakr bought and freed, among them 'Amir ibn Fuhayrah, Umm 'Ubays and Zinnirah.
The quiet starlight of Makkah where the liberated believers gathered in brotherhood.
An Enduring Monument of Honor

Bilal became one of the most honoured Companions. After the call to prayer (adhan) was instituted in Madinah, the Prophet chose him to give it; a report in the books of Sunan says this was because his voice was stronger. Sahih al-Bukhari records that 'Umar ibn al-Khattab used to say: 'Abu Bakr is our master, and he freed our master', meaning Bilal.

Sirah reports relate that on the day of the conquest of Makkah in 8 AH (630 CE), the Prophet told Bilal to climb onto the Kaaba and give the call to prayer. The man who had been tortured on the open ground of Makkah called the adhan from the roof of its sanctuary.
